utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can. I understand you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, Timothy Resch, who is paying us a second visit, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good morning to you as well. And appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, I'm here with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic and it's nice to be back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you. So, yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask to go into private session in a moment just for one matter. But otherwise administratively, Mr. Kirudja, as Your Honour was told, the United Nations gave us permission that he could testify in open session as he testified in Milosevic. We did actually stop the last witness from coming because even if Mr. Kirudja finishes earlier than we anticipate, I would have thought I'll be a day and a half roughly, I'm very bad on estimating how long it takes to get through documents and Mr. Ackerman I understood told -- I've forgotten what it was now but that he thought he would be about the same amount of time if not two days. So given that the witness we had lined up for Friday would have been from Prnjavor and would have gone into quite a lot of the background, it was unlikely we could finish him in the one day. So I don't know -- there may be administrative matters we can deal with on the Friday if we have a spare day. Your Honour, Having said that, may I go into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, Madam usher, could you please bring the witness in? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. I know this is not the first time you're giving evidence in this -- before this Tribunal so I'll go straight to the point. Our rules require that you make a solemn declaration, which is equivalent to an oath, to speak the truth in the course of your testimony before you actually start giving testimony. So I kindly ask you to stand up, take in your hand the text of the solemn declaration and read it out loud and that will be your undertaking with this Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. You may sit down. Ms. Korner will be leading you in her examination-in-chief, and she will be followed by Mr. Ackerman, who is the lead counsel for the Defence later on. Your testimony is expected to last a few days but hopefully, if you stick to the rule that you answer the question, the whole question and nothing but the question, we should be over by Thursday at the latest. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, is your name Charles Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And for a number of years now, have you worked for the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, before I deal with your background -- and I'm almost certainly going to make the same mistake because you and I are both speaking English, the temptation is for you to answer the question the minute that I finish and it's sometimes necessary to have a break so that it can be interpreted for the purposes of the accused in this case. I think you started work for the United Nations in 1977?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you held positions related to development, economics and internal UN budgetary and management matters?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: All of that plus something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that is?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Peacekeeping operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to come on, then, to those peacekeeping operations. In 1988, were you assigned to the UN humanitarian assistance mission for Afghanistan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you serve there as the chief of finance and administration?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In 1992, did you start your service with the UN missions in the former Yugoslavia, working with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And from April, 1992, until March of 1994, did you serve as chief civil affairs officer?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: I started as chief civil affairs officer for a couple of weeks and it was standardised to civil affairs coordinator.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you assigned to begin with to an area, one of the protected areas, known as we'll see in the documents as an UNPA, to Sector North, which was in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you serve there from -- until 1994, after which you went to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then just to complete matters, from August of 1994 until June of 1995, did you serve as the delegate for the special representative of the Secretary-General to the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just to deal very briefly with your educational qualities -- qualifications, sorry, I think you were educated at the university of Nairobi that you have a masters degree from York university in Toronto and a doctorate from the university of Western Ontario?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kirudja, having gone through all of that, can I next deal with your knowledge when you first went to Croatia of the conflict? Did you hold any preconceived ideas about who or what had started the conflict?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: I had no clue who or what had started what.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So did you have any bias towards one side or the other when you arrived in Croatia, namely either the Serbs or the Croatians or whatever?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: None. I even got to know the difference between -- I didn't know there were Serbs, Croats, I think there were Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I think it's right that you arrived in Belgrade in early April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: I think the 6th of April, I arrived in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And pursuant to the Security Council resolutions, was the United Nations stationed in four areas of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as you've already told us, you were assigned to the area called Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: I made a slight detour to getting there. I was first asked to take a tour of Sector West.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think the first thing perhaps we ought to do is to ask you to look at in fact two maps, one which you prepared for the purposes of the case when you were testifying in the Milosevic case. Could you have a look, please, at a map which was -- it says Exhibit 2 in the Milosevic case but it's a black and white one. Perhaps we can have it put on the ELMO. In a moment I'm going to show you a map, which is perhaps slightly clearer, but I think you yourself drew the boundaries of Sector North; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, and you note at the top of that exhibit there is the word "approximate".

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Important, because I did this from memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And we can see that it runs along the Croatian-Bosnian border from roughly speaking Bosanska Dubica, which we can see to the way -- map goes around, all the way down and the last bit really is going off the map. Did it go a bit further than we could actually see on this map?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes. You mentioned the border between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's important that you note that this is what you meant. This is the internationally recognised border.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: That runs up to here, and continues this way, but the sector itself doesn't go all of that part. It turns left this way and this wasn't an international border, isn't an international border. We are now inside Croatia. What is now the nation of Croatia. So this was a confrontation line between the Serbs, who occupied inside this area, and the rest of Croatia. So on this border, the Serbs faced Croatia -- on this international -- on this confrontation line, the Serbs faced Croats. On this side, they faced Muslims and from here the Serbs faced each other, Serbs on this side, Serbs on that side.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Last point, it goes down farther south, off the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So if we just for the purposes of the transcript, where you said Serbs faced each other, if you could just indicate that part again?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes. This is the municipality of Velika Kladusa runs up that way, somewhere up to here, the municipality of Bosnia -- Dvor Na Una begins. And this is -- from here roughly, around here, all the way this border the Serbs faced each other in the municipality of Dvor and in the municipality of Kostajnica they faced each other on both sides of that international border.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the part that you say was Muslim-held was?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: This is the Velika Kladusa, Bihac, Bosanska Krupa, around here, all of this area right here which we normally called Bihac pocket.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: I'm sorry, and the Serbs talking to us called Cazin region.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then I think you have indicated by a cross Topusko where were you based?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: This was our headquarters this is where the mission headquarters in Sector North.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Could that be made, please, Your Honours, P1644? And we will just have a look, because it is slightly clearer, although you didn't use -- draw -- a coloured map which is an extract. Now that just I think it's a slightly clearer and we can see a bit more of Bosnia on that. We can see Topusko marked -- with a mark just above the letter B for Banija?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you look -- it's written across -- if you see where Velika Kladusa is?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then I think we can see Topusko just above it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yeah, there it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then we can see the two pockets, the two parts that you marked, and on this map, we can see clearly Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, Prijedor and then just to the edge of it Banja Luka. Were those names that became familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can I just ask you: Do you yourself ever go over the border into Bosnia and visit any of these places?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes. Particularly in the Bihac pocket.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: I meant -- by that I meant all of this area, this, this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever get to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: No. I didn't have to -- I didn't need to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That will be P1645, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you made a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, you made a couple, in fact, but the first statement was made, I think, over a period in September of 1999. In order to make that statement, did you look at reports prepared by you or persons who you had worked with?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: The representatives of the Prosecutor's Office came into my office in New York with a file.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: A folder -- file that surprised me that there were that many and they were my documents, and they started to talk to me on the basis of those documents and then building that statement themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to that, were you also able to refresh your memory about the events of 1991 and 1992 from notebooks that you yourself had compiled about meetings that you had held and also incidents?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes. As we proceeded from that, it became necessary for me to refer to those what you call diaries, they are my notes, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you just tell Their Honours were these notes that you made during the course of meetings or immediately after incidents that you recorded?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: During the course of the meetings, as I listened, because I had to have a translation, I had interpreters, it made it possible for me to talk at the same time and write my own notes while what we were saying was being translated so it was possible for me to write simultaneously as I was conducting the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, if necessary, Mr. Kirudja, I'm going to ask you to refresh your memory from those notes which I think you've got with you today. Now, can we go back to the beginning of your posting there? I'm sorry, I said 1991. It's just 1992. You've already told us that before you went to Sector North, you carried out a familiarisation tour of Sector West. Can you just -- where was Sector West roughly?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Sector West is also referred to as Western Slavonia. It is -- in this highway of brotherhood called -- somewhere midway between Sector North and Sector East, more or less. Its headquarters was in Daruvar and if you look at the road, the highway, it's more or less above Banja Luka and the other areas that you showed in that map, somewhere above that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Court is actually I think already familiar with Western Slavonia so you needn't explain. Were you then sent by the director of civil affairs, a Mr. Cedric Thornberry to Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, I received a cable while I was still in Sector West to proceed to Sector North.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when you got to Sector North, what were your duties there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Basically, as civil affairs coordinator, my overall responsibilities was to ensure that the totality of the assets of the UN are used as -- in full, as intended under the mandate and that included advisory role to the military sector commander, who, as you would expect, were from outside, unfamiliar with the way the UN does business so I had that part of my responsibility in an advisory capacity to the sector commander on the military side. And on the other side, on the civilian, political side, I had the responsibility of course to see that the basic plan, the Vance plan, that outlined the meetings -- outlined the requirements of the mission was also properly implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That leads me to the next question: What was the Vance plan? What was the intention of that plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: The Vance plan, I can describe it in operational terms as having three principal components. At the very start of the mission, the Vance plan required that all armed units in that area of the United Nations protected force or United Nations Protected Areas, where the United Nations protective force was deployed, all armed units were to totally demobilise, meaning the JNA and any other armed unit, they had to totally demobilise and that would be followed, or rather Vance plan recognised that there was a need for law and order to be kept, so it allowed for a civil police, locally controlled and manned civil police, but the Vance plan only allowed them to have side arms or light weapons, and thirdly, the Vance plan did require that, as the mission progressed, conditions be created both by the local authorities, as well as the UN, so that all the people who had been displaced from there would voluntarily return to the area, and therefore much of our civil side and political side requirements was to make sure that that happened, that the conditions for voluntary return of displaced persons were developed. That in summary were the three elements, the Vance plan required.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when you got to Sector North in April of 1992, what was the situation there? Was the plan going according to -- I was going to say according to plan.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: I understand. I understand what you meant. The conditions were such that the plan was at zero stage. The plan hadn't started. There were already -- there were still the presence of the JNA fully armed and all other armed units in the area, if that's what you're driving at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I am, yes. Rather badly phrased.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: It's all right. I got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it was about to start when you got there. What did that mean that you personally had to do?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: As I said, operationally, the heaviest requirements on our agenda was to meet with all the parties that were necessary to achieve a demobilisation and they came in three parts for my purposes. On the one part, I had of course the United Nations military side, the generals and others from various contingents to deal with in order to make sure that they understood that we now need to get the plan in motion. That on our side. On the local Serbs and Croats side, there were the commanders on the Serb side and the commanders on the Croatian side where they were still facing each other militarily, complete with guns and tanks still facing each other along confrontation line. So the first basic requirement was to go all around wherever they were to begin meetings to find who is who, who controls what and get going on now we are here, let's get this over, let's get you to go back to wherever you came from, and demobilise. That was the immediate requirement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've said that the Serbs and Croats were still facing each other along a confrontation line. What was the attitude of the warring parties towards the intervention by the UN?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: There was a different understanding of -- and that was important, not -- we had to notice that very early, that there was different interpretation, especially between the Serbs and the Croats, as to what they expected us to do. So we come to them on the Serb side, we have maps of -- showing where these United Nations protected area should be. According to the Vance plan, the Vance plan had named opstinas that translates loosely as municipalities, that was the subject of this conflict. They were named in the Vance plan. And those named opstinas comprised either Sector North, Sector East, Sector West, as they were known during the federal Yugoslavia before the conflict. On the Croatian side they interpreted that mean if an opstina is named as part of the sector, then the sector's edge would be defined by the civil boundaries that comprised each opstina at the edge or the way in the rough map that you saw me trace a few minutes ago. And their maps showed that is where you should be deployed as the UN up to the edge of that opstina. The Serb side had a different interpretation of that. They had waged a war and brought it to -- up to where they stopped. There was a reason why they stopped where they stopped, and that is where the confrontation line was. So their map will show the edge of the United Nations Protected Area will correspond to where the confrontation line was, and the difference between those interpretations was immediately an issue and later became known as the pink zones, a subject of a separate United Nations Security Council resolution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, in respect of the disengagement of the JNA from Croatia, who were you dealing with? Who was the general in charge?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: On the Croatian side? On the Croatian side it was a lot more extended and there was a commission for UNPROFOR and that commission for UNPROFOR had both military and civilian components. On the headquarters side very early we had a couple of generals that we dealt with, General Stolnik was one of them, General Cesnjaj was one of them, and at the top of that commission was Dr. Ramljak, the deputy Prime Minister. On the ground, there were different generals because they had organised themselves into different operational zones. In my sector, ranging all the way from commanders located in Sisak, Karlovac, even in Rijeka, had to go to Rijeka because some of the military that controlled the western corner of that sector were based there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about from the Serb side? Who was the military leader that you were dealing with?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: It was much easier for the Serb side because the entire sector, Sector North, came under the 10th corps of the previous JNA, and it was commanded by General Spiro Nikovic who was based in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said that the previous JNA. When you arrived, was it still the JNA?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: It was still the JNA, pardon me for the use of that language, it was still the JNA when we arrived and they were JNA commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, your mandate was for the sector in Croatia, Sector North. At that stage, in April of 1992, was there any operational mandate for Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And at that stage, when you first arrived, had it been foreseen that there was a problem in Bosnia or likely to be a problem in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: When we arrived in retrospect now I can say so, the UN was mistaken. I didn't know we were mistaken when we arrived but we had a premise, we operated on a premise that later proved to be incorrect, that the entire BH would be more peaceful, there was no evident at that time signs of trouble and so even from our headquarters, the structure of the mission was done with the assumption that there would be peaceful circumstances prevailing in Bosnia. To that effect, the headquarters of the mission was supposed to be in Sarajevo, even if the centres where we discussed, the headquarters of the mission was Sarajevo, and the logistics battalions that would serve the missions were to be located in Banja Luka, both the French and the Finnish battalions were supposed to be, and they initially were in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And let's just jump ahead for a moment. Did the Finnish and French battalions remain in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Of course not. Very soon they found it wasn't feasible for them to be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you now about your dealings with the Serb side. What impression did you get about what the objective of the Serbs was?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: In terms of the sector where we were or overall or?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's deal with it in stages. First of all, in terms of the sector where you were.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Like I was saying earlier they had each a misunderstanding of what was going to happen, not only as I explained earlier as regards where the border should be, for the Serbs, they had also the impression that we literally were going to relieve them in their fox holes and I'm not exaggerating on that, when we went in the first meetings, the colonels came over and told the general, okay where are your men coming to relieve mine in the fox holes? So they were surprised when the general told them no one is relieving you from the fox holes, you're leaving the fox holes and getting demobilised and there should be a status quo, no fighting here, no one needs to be relieved. So that was the first surprise that they had. That the UN was not coming designed to fight anyone or to be facing any hostile forces. That was a major learning experience for the Serbs, as they got to know why we were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So that's on the -- now, what about as far as you could tell from your conversations with Serb leaders, what was their general idea that was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: I think I understand maybe. We were then of course listening particularly on the civilian side of the Serb leadership, each opstina had a mayor which was permitted under the Vance plan, and we would hear them very often repeat something pretty early to us that became a focus for me and I heard it repeated. We, the Serbs said early and often, we are convinced we are never going to be able to live together again with non-Serbs. The sooner you, as the UN, understood that, the better there will be for the peace in these areas. We now intend never to live together again with anybody else. You asked me earlier if I knew the Serbs or Croats or whatever the Muslims were, that's when these differences began to register with me, and I said, "What do you mean you're not going to live together with non-Serbs again and you want to live in one country together only for Serbs?" And that's when they began to talk about why they were fighting who and the territory that they had. Specifically, the territory that we were deployed in would be part of that one country that the Serbs wanted to live in. Now, there was no -- a little bit of a non-sequitur for me if you say you're going to live in the same country and as you saw in the map we are only in an United Nations Protected Area, there is an implication that this is bigger than the United Nations Protected Area, where else do you want this country to be?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the Serbs that you were talking to, first of all, were all these Croatian Serbs or were there Bosnian Serbs as well at this stage?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Frankly made no difference to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's put it this way. The people you were meeting were who? Obviously General Ninkovic you've spoken to us about. Who else were you dealing with at this stage, April 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: On the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, not names, just generally.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Okay. It is probably clearer to mention that while the entire sector came under the 10th corps, it was divided, subdivided, if you like into operational zones, each with commanders of their own, and Sector North had two divisions or rather three divisions. There was on the western side of it the Kordun operational zone. That was commanded by a Colonel by the name of Cedo Bulat. On the Banija side not Banja like you spell Banja Luka, Banija side. B-A-N-I-J-A, Banija. This operational zone was at that time commanded by General Rakovic, and there was on the southern tip on the map which I also mentioned went off your map, formed an operational zone called Lika. It was smaller and it was headquartered off my sector in Kornica [phoen]. So there were these commanders in these areas that I had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you also dealing with politicians, local politicians?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said that what was -- what you were hearing was that we Serbs cannot live with other nationalities. And that they wanted to live in one state. Was the term Greater Serbia ever used?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: No. If it appears in my testimony, it probably appears under quotes because we are talking retrospectively.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: So at that stage it's more accurate, I heard more often one state rather than Greater Serbia, more or less like we are going to -- we would like to live only among ourselves as Serbian nation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, the withdrawal that was supposed to be taking place, I want to deal with this quite shortly, but what was happening in respect of the demilitarisation of that particular zone?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Now, to go back on, we would say to the commander at that time General Nikovic, we need a schedule, and an identification of the units, weapons, and the schedule about when you will demilitarise this particular sector, we did get that schedule within the weeks of April, May, somewhere around there, that schedule, and General Nikovic did outline all the units that were to be demobilised, and the weapons. But he did also explain -- during the course of that, he did also give us an idea noticing we are strangers here to give us an idea of what was happening and why, and he mentioned certain things that still at that time didn't get lost to us, as important. He said we have a new reality, things like that, new reality happening in the former Republic of Yugoslavia. We are going to demobilise from this area. Our headquarters in Belgrade has decided that as we demobilise, all command officers that run the JNA who were not born in these areas where we are now will have to leave these areas and the command of whatever is left here will be in the hands of Serbs who were born there, either in the area where we were or other areas across in Bosnia that were still under his command. But he also went on to say, when we are all done, from what used to be the former Yugoslavia, will arise seven countries and he proceeded to name them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at a couple of reports that you made about this. First of all, could you have a look at a report dated the 30th of April? The document number is document number 12 -- 2. Can we just check? No, no, no, no. It's the document -- it's document 2 which should be the -- it should be the fourth document -- right. Can I just check before we -- yes, I think it's much easier if I check before you take it up. Yes, that's it. Thank you. The reports that you wrote, would that be on a weekly basis or on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: They had a variety. This particular one, for example, would be of the category where I would write an immediate report for that day, after the meeting, because it would be something I wanted reported immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: And then at the end of the week, I would also write what was a generalised situational report that was freer in framework but more of a raw understanding for that week. So there were that category of reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this particular report, was that a special report, because of this meeting that you'd had?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In addition to that, did you make notes of this meeting in your what I'm going to call your diary?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: In other words my diaries were the basis of compiling the report. They are related that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask you if you can find that part because I think you may need it in respect of some of the conversations. Now, --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: This report is on 30th April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think as we'll see it related to a meeting on the 29th.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now if we look at first of all, the report, it states that it's -- there was a meeting with General -- I think it should be Ninkovic although it says Nikovic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: No, from the early days I always referred to him in his presence as Nikovic. If I was in error he was very kind to me and let that error persist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was a meeting in Bihac and then you listed in your report the issues of political and civil affairs interest. And that you recorded in paragraph 2 that "General Ninkovic announced that as of the day before, there was a new Yugoslavia comprising the republics of Serbia and Montenegro." And he said he would continue as a general and soldier of his new country. "This development while posing some political problems of uncertainty also may pose some new practical problems, particularly in Serbian Krajina and in Bosnia, clearly the JNA does not belong in the area after the new political reality." Can I ask two questions please on that paragraph? What was the practical problems that you foresaw in the Serbian Krajina? And by Serbian Krajina were you talking about that part that was on the Croatian side or the Bosnian side?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: A clarification, as I respond to your question. Among the new countries that were to arise from the former Yugoslavia that he proceeded to name was what he called the Republic of Serbian Krajina. All the others remained as named as the constituent republic, Slovenia, Croatia, Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, but he added Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: At that time, you realise that that was a problem of a practical nature because first, where was this Serbian Krajina going to be? If it was inside the UNPAs, we have a problem because under the Vance plan, there were no recognised authorities that overarched the opstinas, there was not to be an overall government that connected these opstinas. Under the Vance plan, the highest authority in each location was the civil government of the opstina comprising the mayor and the chief of police and police armed with the light weapons. There was no overarching authority like a government of Serbian Krajina, that would pose a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So can we just recap so that we understand because I think this comes from your notebook rather than the report. He told you that of the republics of Serbia and Montenegro -- the new Yugoslavia, and then what did he actually go on to say? Could you read just what your note says?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes. There will be six countries out of the former Yugoslavia, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I'm sorry I said seven. My note says six countries and they are named, he named as follows: Slovenia, Croatia, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, what was Serbia and Montenegro, Serbian Krajina, Macedonia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, which he did not characterise any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, just for a moment, we look at what you report to --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Excuse me one more thing he said on the note, and I quote, "The government agreement with Republic of Yugoslavia, what UNPROFOR agrees with the Belgrade will apply to the Republic of Serbian Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And what did you understand him to be saying there? As a matter of political reality, what did that mean?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: This was his serving notice that since in that meeting, bear in mind we are discussing about demobilisation and what to do, it was his reassurance to us that what we agree in these meetings, I'm an officer of the JNA, I report to Belgrade, it will apply to this area you are which is the Serbian Republic of Krajina. That's what he meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You already I think mentioned that, and you referred to it in the second paragraph of your report, one of the options in consideration is that all JNA officers and personnel not born in Serbian Krajina or Bosnia-Herzegovina will be advised to leave for the new Yugoslavia, thus all soldiers born in this region will be left behind with all necessary equipment and weapons as a counterbalance to the Croatians who are now strengthening their position. And I think you already mentioned that. Now, the rest of this report, I think, is concerned about the mechanics, was it not, of how they were going to -- how the JNA was going to withdraw?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And could you just look, please, at the last paragraph of that report which begins, "The recent emergence of a newly fortified militia is hard not to notice. Former military vehicles have been repainted from green to blue. The colours of the present police force -- sorry, the colours of the present police force. Many of the militiamen have begun to support -- sorry, sport new blue uniforms and appear to be deployed along the front line. The JNA side seems to be taking advantage of the Vance plan which apparently excludes police units from those that must be demobilised and their weapons put in storage." The significance of this being what?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Serve notice to my headquarters, there is a loophole in the Vance plan, and that loophole, the Serbs are -- have already begun to notice the outlines that they were going to exploit that loophole to make the demobilisation of the forces difficult to achieve, and since they were allowed to keep a police force, they would now transform what is essentially a fighting -- a military fighting unit into, for the purposes of satisfying the Vance plan, into a police force which is only a police force in name, because it has the fighting capability of a military force. That is the implication.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In other words, the police force was being, as you say here, was being given military vehicles. Was it also being provided with arms?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: This point, two things were happening. We are trying to identify the arms for the purposes of a requirement of the Vance plan, that they be decommissioned, all these armaments that were there after demobilisation of personnel, they were to be put in storage under a two lock system, UNPROFOR and the local authorities would have a key and you needed double for that purposes. So at this moment, the weapons, while we are trying to identify them the purposes of decommissioning, we are also noticing that they are being redistributed and being put to use but under the police. That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, finally on this meeting, did you raise with the general the problems of, as it were, refugees in Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes. I had been called to the Croatian side. There was a football, a soccer field in Karlovac, because there is an another football field matter, I don't want to confuse your train of thought with, they had gathered in Karlovac a lot of people and they wanted to go across the sector into Bihac pocket and they had stated to me, -- I went there physically to see them. They had all vehicles some with the licence plates in Austria and other distant places from Croatia and they were Muslims, those who spoke to me, and -- the majority of them and they want go back to the Bihac pocket and would I make it possible for them through the sector to Bihac pocket? And I said to General Nikovic as much. These people wanted to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was his response to that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: General Nikovic was given to colourful language and so he said, "Well, if they come here, we will give them a concert."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you got a note in your diary about this. Can you just tell us what his exact words were?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: What date, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 29th again, it's the same meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Okay. He said -- as soon as I explained what I say to you, I wrote his response was, "I want to tell you never, we will not allow that. They say they are Muslims. They are not. They are trained in Austria, Germany, to fight. We will prepare a concert for them."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You had seen the people. Did they strike you, from your conversations with them, as people who were trained fighters, who wanted to go into Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Hard to say by looking at them, because they were in all regard civilians in civil clothes but if you look at them as human beings and ask are they capable of suddenly putting military uniforms, are they able bodied and all of that, the answer of course would be they are healthy, they are normal and that would be --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were they just single men or were they families?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: These were mostly men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, that was that meeting. Did the process that you referred to, this handing over of weapons and military vehicles to the police, continue?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: This process continued in terms of what we on our military side wanted, and we were expecting the schedule that General Nikovic had put out to be executed on the Serb side. It wasn't completely because by 10th of May, around 10th of May, I notice in my report somewhere the date might be not quite in my original but my notes tells me it was around the 10th of May, General Nikovic when we went to see him gave us what we considered a bomb shell. "I'm no longer in command."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we are going to look at that later on. All right. Now, I think you recorded, is this correct, one other incident involving as it were the first persons you'd met who left Bosnia on the 30th of April, when you noted down a particular car.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, oh, yes. That family. It was the first, to our surprise, indication that all was not well, both in the sector as well as in Bosnia, when a family arrived in distress and it arrived in -- that family arrived in Sector North to hostile reception by the Serbs. That's how it got to our notice. A man, a woman and a child. If that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you make a note about this in your diary?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes. Because we then set out to protect them from the harassment that immediately started on the Serb authorities, the family was known as the Cakar family. I remember after looking at the notes just this week, they had a car registered in Neuchatel in Switzerland. The particulars I took on their travelling documents, passport and what have you, also indicated that the husband of this family was of a Turkish origin. The wife was of a local, was a -- born in Bosanski Novi, and they had gone to Bosanski Novi, either to visit or something, and they were coming out of there in distress.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the distress was caused by what?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: They were not going to talk to me as much at that stage about Bosanski Novi. What they were concerned with was the fact that the local Serbs in Sector North wanted them to kind of leave the car there or move out of there and they felt literally insecure. I for one didn't understand it because we are there, it is an UN place, there is nobody fighting up to that moment and I wondered why the chiefs of police in Vojnic, where they had landed were harassing them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And in fact, were you obliged to employ the UN civil police?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Outside their hotel room?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Indeed. I called the chief of civil police, a Danish, by the name, Kai Vittrup, and he went into action and all night posted guards in their hotel and made arrangements for the next day that we would evacuate them in a kind of protection, we sandwiched their cars between ours and we got them out into Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to move then please next to a meeting on the 4th of May, which again I think you recorded in your diary. Oh, yes, I'm sorry, Your Honour, may I make document 2 Exhibit P1646? That's the one of the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: You say the 4th of May?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 4th of May, when I think you had another meeting with General Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: All right. Yes, I note that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And again, was this a meeting really about the boundaries?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: This was a continuation of the issue of who -- identification of what unit had to be demobilised and what schedule was there for the -- for that to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you record in your diary something about General Ninkovic's mood?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes. While we came to talk about that subject, the one I mentioned about demobilisation, and for my record he had given us the dates -- just a minute. Usually my notes have a lot of things on them so it takes sometime to locate a particular subject. I beg your pardon. You're talking about his mood?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think did you record that he was in a bad mood and he gave you an explanation, I think, for it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: I know about that. I knew he was in a bad mood and I knew why. I'm trying to find out whether it was on the 4th of May or not, simply that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It could be the 5th?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: That's all I'm trying to find. I know the mood and why. I'm just trying to figure out whether it was May or not on the particular meeting. Anyway, whatever date it is I can tell you what it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you can recall it tell us what he told you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: He was particularly in a bad mood because, as a soldier, he followed everything, and around a few days before that meeting, there was a reported in the news event in Sarajevo resulting to the death of certain of his colleagues and he knew them personally and he was quite upset about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did he mention anything about any projected unrest or aggression in the Krajina area? You may need to find your note on this.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Unless -- at least, more specific about that, about the unrest, more specificity about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: See if you can find in your note --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour if there is no objection I can lead this from his statement. Unless there is an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you any objection, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I basically have an objection to everything that's been going on since 9.00 because we are dealing with Croatia which has nothing to do with this indictment and I don't know why we are spending all this time in Croatia. It seems totally irrelevant. But within that context, if the Court believes we should go forward with Croatia, then I don't have any objection to what Ms. Korner proposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour this is the background and the build up. This part is indistinguishable, April, May, from what is Bosanski Novi was right on the border and that's why it's linked in with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. You have our authorisation to lead on this on this matter and on this matter only.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did -- I think he came and as you say, he explained about what he described as JNA soldiers being massacred in Sarajevo. And did he also tell you that he had some information that the other side wants to commit some type of aggression on the Krajina sometime before the 15th of May?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And it was always something hinted. This is not even new. In the other report, you mentioned and you saw quoted that we had to leave some weapons because there will be future attacks. So this was just illustrating a point made over and over again as a ground why they were going to leave certain weapons around.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, also, at that meeting, did he tell you that that morning, Yugoslavia had called its citizens to leave JNA units in Bosnia and to return to the Yugoslav territory?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes. This is the 5th of May meeting?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And did he explain that according to him, the JNA will not have any influence in Bosnia from now on?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That there were only a few officers, some 13, in the JNA that remain in Croatia and Bosnia who were from Yugoslavia. All the others are Bosnian Serbs or Krajina Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Those officers and soldiers not from Bosnia or Croatia will be sent back to Yugoslavia. Serbian forces in Bosnia will thus establish their own military and arms and weapons in Bosnia, will be in the hands of the local Serbs under the new system.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yeah, you're reading my notes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm reading from your statement but that's clearly from your notes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then he finally ends up by saying when all of this happens, 80 per cent of Bosnian territory will be under the control of Serbian units?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think he also added 93 per cent of the 10th corps of the JNA are local Serbs of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did he go on to say, and I think we can deal with this quite briefly, that the JNA has problems because some local units do not want to give up their weapons?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: This was important, even on that -- and you might see it related to other things. Here he is a soldier who had agreed to do what the United Nations requested of him, but it was clear he was himself subject to opposition for doing that, for the schedule and the means by which he wanted to demobilise. He was, fair to say, facing resistance for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And facing resistance from whom, did you understand?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: It wasn't clear until much later when he had left and that was clear that there was something called Territorial Defence forces that wanted to do something different from what he had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, if we can then deal, I think briefly, on the 10th of May you had this meeting with him and is that when he told you that he was being retired and that the temporary commander in Sector North would be General Rakovic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: That is precisely the point. Here, the schedule that he had put out was to be completed by, when you are talking I already saw the dates in my notes was to be completed by the 23rd of May. On the 10th of May, he announces that he is retired, he's been retired, while he was scheduled to meet with us to complete this. Now, that doesn't stand to reason. If you are going to demobilise, if you're a soldier, you have two weeks and as a schedule. It doesn't stand to reason that you will be terminated three weeks before you wind down an operation. That's why I said there was resistance to what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, next, and this is now we see how events developed over the border. Could you have a look, please, at a document which is document 4? Can you just tell us what that is, the type of document, rather?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: This is a daily situation report from -- from our headquarters, and they made a military -- military side as opposed to my civilian side, they would make a daily situation report. This is one of -- one such report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is that dated the -- it's quite difficult to tell but is it the 8th of May or 11th of May?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: No it's 11th -- 23rd -- what is this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's quite difficult to work out but in any event can we just --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: No. It's the time, the military they also put a date and the hour, 2300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it's the 11th of May at 2300 hours?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we look at under item 2(B), the chief of police in Dvor and gives the grid reference, Mr. Nikola Bjelac reported to DanCon, is that the Danish battalion?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: No, Danish contingent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Contingent, sorry. Danish contingent, that Serbians in militia uniform had crossed to Dvor to disarm all Muslim militia in Bosanski Novi. Can you remember now, was that the first time that you became aware of potential problems involving Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: I can't be sure it's the first time, and it underscores a point I made earlier when I was describing that map when I said Serbs faced each other across the border, whether it was in the Croatian side or Bosanski Novi and I also mentioned that border was nominal, it really didn't matter at all when they faced each other and this report is underscoring that they would cross over from one side to the other routinely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then just very briefly, because this is another area that's of interest in this trial, under 3, continuing affairs, situation concerning DanCon vehicles in Bosanska Krupa unchanged. Just very briefly, Mr. Kirudja, what did that refer to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: You wouldn't know too much about that one line because that one line was an issue that occurred back when the Nambiar had come visiting the sector, when he was leaving, he was escorted by a military convoy. At the head of that convoy was DanCon vehicles, military vehicles, a Danish [unintelligible] issue. As soon as they were going home to Bosanska Kostajnica, across on the other side of Bosnia, their vehicles were, the convoy was stopped and their vehicles were taken by force by the Serbs and they were always trying to trace where those vehicles were going, and they kept this matter going until much later, they traced those vehicles painted blue under the police in Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And just so the Court understands, Nambiar, was that General Nambiar?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, Satish Nambiar, he had come to visit our sector and that's when the sequence of events I described occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, may that please be made Exhibit P1647?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move then next to -- well, Your Honour, in fact that may be a -- because I'm moving to another meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I just raise a matter before you rise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I would like to request that -- that copies be made of these diaries and notebooks that the witness is referring to and furnished to the Defence and I'm a bit distressed that hasn't happened already. They should have been translated I would think because my client will not be able to assist me in looking at them at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These are otherwise privileged documents, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this is totally unfair, they are not privileged to the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor gets to sit with the witness and go through those and pick out the parts of those diaries that are helpful to the Prosecutor's case and I don't get to look at them or the parts that might be helpful to my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are privileged documents, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They are not privileged if they are using them in court. Once they bring them in court, then they should be available to both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's being made use of in court doesn't remain privileged because it's being made use of in court but the rest which is not being made use of in court remains privileged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I object very strongly to these being used without them being furnished to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want a ruling, file a proper motion and we will decide it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's completely unfair.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the witness can leave and I'll deal with the situation very briefly. We needn't have this discussion in front of the witness but I think we an ought to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 25 minute break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Would Your Honour just -- if the witness is allowed to leave now and Your Honour just remains while I very quickly deal with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I take my privileged documents with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this issue came up in the Milosevic case as well, and His Excellency Judge May made a clear ruling that these were his privileged documents. However it became clear to me when I looked at the statement and I looked at the reports that he must have been relying on the notebook for the purposes of making the statement. I don't think we can make inquiries of him there should be any objection to Mr. Ackerman having copies of the relevant entries on which he based his statement but I think he'd have to show cause why he's entitled to look at any other part of what is the witness's confidential diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The fact is that what is privileged remains privileged. I do understand that it's most uncomfortable and in a way difficult to digest but the fact remains that these are privileged documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think he's entitled, Mr. Ackerman I'm not going to object to that. Mr. Ackerman is certainly entitled to look at or have copies of the pages which he's used to refer to to make the statement but I don't think he's entitled to plough through the rest of it because he's an UN employee and these are UN governmental affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it appears to me, and if I'm wrong, Ms. Korner can correct me, but it appears to me that this witness has basically made these documents available to the Prosecutor and persons who work for the Prosecutor so that they could pick out those parts of them that they think are important so he waived the privilege with regard to the Prosecutor and people who work for the Prosecutor but asserts the privilege with regard to the Defence and people who work for the Defence. I don't think that's fair. And I don't think it's proper. I don't think it can be done. Once he waves it with regard to any party in this case, then if seems to me the documents are -- should be made available to all parties in the case. One party should not have that kind of a totally unfair, unwarranted advantage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you are assuming that he has made available the entirety of those diaries. I'm not assuming anything unless someone comes forward and tells me, yes, I just handed these diaries to the Prosecution so that they could go through the entire entries and decide for themselves what was relevant and what was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I believe that to be true. I believe if you inquire of the Prosecutor you'll find out that that's true, not that he handed them to them but that they went through them with him together and they were able to look at every page if they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in any case if that happened that is covered by the rules while the rules do not cover the right of the Defence to claim copies of those privileged documents, once they remain privileged. You are of course perfectly entitled to ask the witness later on whether he has particularly -- particular entries in his diary relating to this and this and that and that, but it will still depend on him whether he wants to give you that information, because the document remains privileged.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as with all these witnesses, as Your Honour knows originally, this was all going to be in closed session because of the background. Your Honour, I can say that Mr. Kirudja, when I went through the statement, had his diaries in front of him and I asked, can you check in your diaries where this comes from in your statement? As Your Honour will see the statement was taken in 1999. Neither person who works who took the statement works with us any longer so I don't know how it came to be taken but I can certainly say that is what happened when I spoke to him before the -- before he came to give evidence but Your Honours, I'm certainly -- Mr. Ackerman wants him to check his diary to see if there is any entry in relation to anything Mr. Ackerman is interested in, he will but I don't think Mr. Ackerman can just fish through the diaries to see if there is anything that may be of interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. 25 minute break, which means we start at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour just before the witness is brought back in again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just go for a moment to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go to private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open -- no, we are still in private session. We are in open session now. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the other thing I've noticed and it may be a bit difficult because there is no B/C/S version of course, those in the public gallery, and we have the odd person here, none of the documents are going up on the ELMO so that the gallery doesn't know what on earth anybody is talking about. I'm not sure whether we've got -- have we got any spare ones? Anyhow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can make available one of our three copies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just noticed of course that we had some people here this morning because there is only one English version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that. We can make available and we can share, all right? We will do that, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I think we can use -- of course Ms. Gustin has a copy so we can use ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I want to move now, please, to mid-May, the 19th of May. I think you had a meeting at the request of the community of Bihac, and subsequently, I think you prepared or one of your staff prepared a report on that. So could you have a look, now, please, at document which was number 5 but it's actually sorry, P1658? It's already been placed into the bundle. Now, Your Honour, there has been a slight hiccup on this, as usual, I'm afraid, which is my fault entirely. In the bundle we only have the first two pages of that report or the cover sheet. The actual document itself is considerably longer. It contained a report dated the 20th of May, as well as the -- and it didn't go into the Novi bundle because it wasn't specifically referable to Novi but the original document produced by Mr. Kirudja had quite a lengthy report. Now I don't know whether Your Honours had Mr. Kirudja's documents. You didn't. All right. Can I perhaps for the moment put this in with it on the ELMO? Mr. Kirudja can see it coming up and we will make sure there are copies availability after the next break. I think Mr. Ackerman who did get the original Kirudja document, the report dated Sector North 20th of May, 1992, do you have that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, this is the one in my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, don't worry about that there's another report Mr. Kirudja, which I'm afraid...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well it looks like I may only have the same, the first two pages. There is a couple of additional pages here but they seem to be different print, different numbering and but also seems to be 20 May. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, they are -- Mr. Ackerman got the whole bundle of disclosures from Mr. Kirudja I don't know how long ago whenever we disclosed the documents, for the moment, 25th of June, 2001. But can I put this on the ELMO and then I'll arrange for copies to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then usher, can you put -- I'm going to have to look at it on the ELMO as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, it's going to go on the ELMO, and if you can -- perhaps actually can I have mine back for a moment and we will put this one on. Thank you. This report which runs to three pages, I'm sorry, usher, could we go to the third page and just look at the signature for a moment on the ELMO? It's signed by a gentleman named Paolo Raffone deputy chief civil affairs office, was he one of your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now can we go to the first page, please? If we just pull it down, yeah. It's dated the 20th of May, 1992, subject, note on the situation in the Bihac area, border of Bosnia with Sector North, and its possible influence on Sector North political analysis. Geographic and ethnic outlook, it describes the Bihac area and then says, "The majority of the 250.000 inhabitants of the Bihac area are mainly Muslims. Bihac 66.6 per cent, Cazin 97.6 and then Bosanska Krupa, 74.5. No ethnic Serbs are reported to live in this area." Then it deals with the infrastructures and then if we look at the political analysis, if you pull it up for a moment, please, usher, a bit further up, sorry, thank you. "The representatives of the Bihac community explained that their major commercial partner was the Republic of Croatia. Nowadays they feel that Croats and Muslims can fight together against the common enemy, the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. As a matter of fact, this area has remained quite calm compared with the rest of BH. New developments could be envisaged following the rapid worsening of the living conditions. Many persons identify emotionally, the Serbs as the only cause of their difficulties. For this reason, factions and groups could oppose themselves to the Serbs in the RSK as well as BH." And then I'm going to summarise this: You -- Mr. Raffone explained the reason for this feeling about the Serbs, including the withdrawal of the JNA from the area has also contributed to stress or resentments against the ethnic Serbs. Then can we go to the next page, please? Where Mr. Raffone noted that as a matter of fact, the area was suffering a very strict blockade in all directions. It is very rare to meet commercial trucks in the streets. The authorities of this area recognise openly that their region is encircled and that they suffer a blockade. The authorities in the RSK do not have the same attitude. I would like to underline that both areas suffer -- I think that must be from the same scarcity of supplies and both are blockaded. Then he -- Mr. Raffone identified the interests undertaking the present blockade. Croatia had no interest in taking any action in the about Bihac region, the majority of Croats living there have already fled. These Muslims are fresh forces to join against the Serbs in BH. And the majority of them could join the Green Berets, in Sarajevo. Can I pause there for a moment, please, Mr. Kirudja, the term Green Berets, was that a term that you were familiar with?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then there was further about Croatia. And then this: "Serbia initially tried to open a way [corridor] in northern BH to join the Serb enclaves [the historical Greater Serbia!]." This concept of a corridor, was that something that by the 20th of May, you were familiar with?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: This was the beginning of it because the Serbs who were also in the sector needed to or often would make trips outside of the sector and many of them would tell me we are going to Belgrade, and this corridor became part of their lexicon very early.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And so what -- when you say became part of the lexicon, was that something that was being mentioned to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, we spoke of it as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then it goes on to -- the report, the establishment of the UNMOs and the understanding of this plan by some countries contributed to prevent the final attack. Serbia is appearing cooperative withdrawing the JNA Serbs from the area. And then the resignation of 38 high officers by -- in the JNA could demonstrate that the plan as it was originally conceived has been abandoned by the Serbian leadership. The strategic importance of the area is still considered by Serbia. As a matter of fact, once the majority of Muslims will flee from the northern part of BH towards the south, Serbia might be compensated with these territories, creating a sanitary corridor around the BH Muslims. And brackets, the SRK, I imagine should be the RSK, and Serbia might be reunited. And then I think it deals with humanitarian aid. Now, at this stage, 20th of May, when this report was written, was it becoming evident that there was going to be some kind of problem in respect of these, as it were now, ethnic areas, the Muslims in Bihac and the Serbs on the other side?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, it's the intent of the report was precisely that. I tasked them, as I mentioned earlier, at this moment I was extremely occupied with military matters of disengagement between different parties. Yes, it became clear that that pocket was going to be a major, major concern of ours and we wanted to know as much as we needed to know. And so I tasked him and some other people working with our military to produce a -- such a background report that also was informative and indicative of things that we were already noticing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now can we look, please, at the document we do all have copied, which was your covering sheet to this report, dated the 26th of May? And it's headed, "Subject, potential refugees displaced persons at Bos Novi, Bosanski Novi. UNPROFOR has been informed that up to 5.000 persons in the area of Bosanski Novi may be attempting to get out of the area, to destinations outside of Bosnia. Main conveyor of the information is Mr. Pasic, the mayor of Bosanski Novi. According to third-hand information, all 5.000 are Muslims who have been promised by Serbs that they could be guaranteed a safe passage through the UNPA and to designations in Germany and Austria. They are said to be tired of war, in quotes, and want to leave voluntarily, also in quotes. Will appreciate if UNHCR could assist in obtaining accurate and first-hand information on the story. UNPROFOR would also be grateful for advice and cooperation with UNHCR on handling the issue. We have indications that this story may have other political ramifications. And your earliest action are most appreciated." Was -- this was addressed to whom?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: This was addressed to the headquarters of UNHCR in Zagreb to our liaison office in Banja Luka, as I remember saying to you we had a presence at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
