utterances.text: And my reporting boss, Mr. Thornberry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, how had this information come to you, directly from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: The indicative paragraph there is paragraph 2, according to third-hand information. By that, I mean, look at that date, 26th of May, by then, it is a reference to a meeting I had in Dvor with the mayor of Dvor. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: And that is the mayor of Dvor in the course of my regular other meetings that I mentioned, that stops my agenda and says, "I have a request to make of you." My colleague, the mayor of Bosanski Novi, has informed me there will be these 5.000 people and they would like to make of you certain requests be made. At that moment, I characterised that information to him as third-hand, because it is the mayor of Bosanski Novi, a Serb, reporting what he discussed with the mayor of Bosanski Novi [sic] another Serb, about Muslims who wanted to leave. That is the meaning of third-hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, did you make a note again in your notebook of this meeting that you held on the 26th of May?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you may need to refresh your memory from that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Yes, I have it. It was about 1500 hours in Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you've mentioned the mayor of Dvor, and I don't think we need to go through the list of people but were there other people also present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: No. This was purely inside my sector. We were there for some Vance plan business and so the mayor says to me -- well, there were other people in terms of UN.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what I mean, sorry, yes, there were other people in terms of the UN?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then the mayor of Dvor spoke to you, did he, about this matter from the mayor of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, in a process of making two requests to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour just to get the transcript correct, page 48, line 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Says he spoke to the mayor of Bosanski Novi, a Serb, who spoke to the mayor of Bosanski Novi, another Serb. I think he meant to say or maybe did say that Dvor, the second one was the mayor of Dvor, not both mayor of Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree. It's just an error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Couldn't have been two mayors of Bosanski Novi or one person with a split personality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're right, I meant there were two individuals, separate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For a moment I thought it was a case of schizophrenia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No it was in the context of putting in the context the meaning of third-hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the mayor told you that the mayor of Dvor let's get this straight told you that the mayor of Bosanski Novi wanted passage through the Krajina for Muslims on route to I think you said Austria and Germany.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he tell you what they, the Dvor authorities, had decided to do?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: I want to underscore, he told me we, we collectively, had agreed this was what we want to happen, meaning he in Dvor and his counterpart in Bosanski Novi, and he said because we want these 5.000 people to pass through, I want to make two requests of you, not whether or not we are decided but these two requests had nothing to do with that, is, we have agreed and we want you to do these two things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what were the two things that they wanted you to do?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: First, and I quote, "We want the whole thing filmed by international TV and ensure that the convoy passes through Krajina with full safety. Second, we would like UNPROFOR and the Red Cross to take care of the whole convoy in transit through Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was your response to this? You generally, the UN.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: The first thing for me was what is -- I already characterised that as third hand in my -- in my understanding of it. So that my first reaction was we are in a different jurisdiction, we are in Sector North, part of Croatia, you are the mayor, yes, it is Serb-controlled but a different jurisdiction nevertheless. You are now saying to me that you have agreed, you the mayor of Dvor, have agreed with another mayor across the international border that you will have these 5.000 people getting out of here and through the sector. The first idea of course, something wrong with it. So and I said, and again, at that time, I had no opinions one way or another, I had to maintain diplomatic relations with him. All I said is hint to him something is not right about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you tell him how this would be regarded by the international community?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Exactly. The moment he said now he also said at that meeting, this, Mr. Kirudja, should understand these people are leaving voluntarily. That's the first clue to me. And I say explain to me who are these people? They are Muslims. And I said to him, where they coming from? They are coming from such and such a location, we can get that in details later: And I said in other words they are in their homes? Yes. How do ordinary people voluntarily leave their comfort of their homes and go to far away places? That didn't seem to add up. And that's when he realised that I'm not buying the premise of the story. So he started now explaining to me things to help me get over that initial incredulity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what he explained to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: First these people are leaving because they did not want to fight. They are people who do not want to fight. I said fight who? And they say first we had offered to have them leave that area, Bosanski Novi, to central Bosnia, in places like Zenica, and they refused, he explained. Again, why do you want them to leave their homes, I insisted. And began now bottom line was, we have a new reality, he said to me. And I said what? We have a government of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. First time I ever heard about that. And I said, and? And the people, these people, would not swear allegiance to that government. And that was as far as at that day I wanted to take the issue, and those were the elements that began to build on my mind, and that what explains why that voluntarily in my written memo is between quotes. There were elements telling me, now it doesn't look voluntary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you said that the -- these people, the -- who voluntarily wanted to leave, had -- would not swear allegiance to that government. Was that the government, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia or to a lower level, to Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: The detail of all that didn't come on that meeting. I want to stress.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: The elements that came in that initial meeting was they do not want to fight for Mr. Izetbegovic army, his words. Secondly, we have a government of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and they don't want to fight, don't want to swear allegiance to this government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you ask how the mayor of Dvor could speak on behalf of -- or he and his counterpart in Novi could speak on behalf of the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Exactly. That was the element that I wanted to underscore to him, that you are here now talking to me as a Serb. I remember my exact language was to flatter him, I told him usually you sound to me as a foreigner very convincing when you are explaining to me about Serbs, about their plight, about what concerns you as Serbs. Now, you're telling me about what concerns Muslims indirectly through another Serb mayor in Bosanski Novi. That doesn't sound to me very, very authentic. And at that moment, he realised that I wasn't buying this story and since we were meeting just outside his office, someone or him, I think it is him maybe some other person runs into the mayor's office and the next thing I know is he is holding a telephone and saying to me, here is the mayor of Bosanski Novi, if you want to talk to him if you don't believe us he will tell him himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you speak to the mayor of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: No, not at that moment. My instincts was to try to discourage that story. I really did not want to deal with that story at that moment and I thought by not agreeing to talk to the mayor of Bosanski Novi, this thing that looked very badly thought in at that initial moment it looked like something they were not serious about, if I don't talk to him it will go away so I don't want to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you tell -- and I should perhaps ask you, what was the name of the mayor of Dvor, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, yeah, Jugoslav Borojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you explain to Mr. Borojevic what the international community would think of this evacuation of 5.000 people?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Again, at this moment I gave him a hint, this is not going well with us. I didn't want to go into all that details, all I wanted to serve notice to him at that point, I'm not really going along these lines. So in this initial meeting I only gave him a hint that I am not buying the story.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was it that led you in your own words not to buy the story? What struck you as odd?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: The fact that he is speaking for the Muslims, and he is talking in terms of we are being kind to them, we are being -- we are trying to get to be sure that we ensure their safety, except he's telling me we are also organising them to leave their homes, those two things don't add up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, as a result, you wrote that report, I mean that note that we can see, in fact I think the same day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour then I'm moving on so may that report -- that part of the report, the two pages, is P1658 already. May I ask that the extra bit which we now do have copies available be separately exhibited, well actually, no, Your Honour, that's what I'm asking. I wonder if it can be exhibited as P1658-1 because it's part of the same report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there are now copies available. Don't worry, in English anyhow, the translation is yet to arrive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, as you've explained, you declined to speak to the mayor of Bosanski Novi but the following day, on the 27th of May, did -- was a meeting held with the mayor of Bosanski Novi and somebody from UNHCR? I think we can help you look at please --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, I know the details I can tell you right away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Wait I'm going to give you the document for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Korner, going back some months to UNHCR, is this person that could be named or is he a person that -- whose name ought to be protected?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, can we go into private session for a moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes exactly. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1660. We are in open session now. And as agreed, Mr. Kirudja, you will not refer to this person by his name but just refer to this person as the representative of the other UN organisation. That's it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry we are going to get the document, I hope, P1660.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the first document, Mr. Kirudja, I think, again, is your cover sheet headed, "Subject, 5.000 inhabitants of Bosanski Novi" and then further to my message please find the attached four-page memorandum from the UN organisation representative. And then I think we see the cover from the gentleman, the cover letter from the gentleman who conducted the meeting, and then we come to the actual report itself. Now, I think it's right that you weren't actually present at this meeting but you saw the report before obviously before it was submitted by you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Okay. To get this clear, this report, the author of this report, from UNHCR is the one I shall refer to as the representative of the UNHCR, the author of this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Now, you also mentioned a meeting and you said that I wasn't in it. What meeting are you referring to specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you look at the report of the meeting on the -- it's headed May the 28th but I think as we'll see later it was the 27th of May?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Oh, this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You weren't present at that meeting, were you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: He actually mentions my name that I was there in the first paragraph inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Hmm. All right. In that case, you definitely were there. Sorry, I must be in error in my note. All right. The report begins with a background how it came to your attention?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 2, in the morning of the 28th of May, the mayor of Bosanski Novi, Mr. Radomir Pasic, and a member of the executive council, Mr. Rade, arrived at the headquarters in Topusko for further discussion on the matter. And then it goes on to say that the gentleman who wrote the report had been invited to participate in the meeting. Now, can I just ask you -- did -- were you at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Right. A little correction on the report of this gentleman and also to place it in context, where we were, what he was. We were in my office in Topusko. The date is not quite as he says. It was on 27th. The day after my meeting in Dvor. The one we spoke to you about. Immediately the day after. Thirdly, this gentleman was stationed inside my office at my request from UNHCR very early, earlier on in April, I went to Zagreb and knowing the importance of refugees and the way the UN handles it, it was understood that we needed a resident representative of UNHCR in my office. Therefore, in all meetings where the issue of refugees were, I will just say go and get that gentleman immediately into the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. You're absolutely right, it's my error you were at this meeting. It's a later one I got muddled with because I think you also; is that right, made a note of that meeting in your diary?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, first of all, at what's contained in this actual written report? Summary paragraph 3, summary and present status, the request from Bosanski Novi essentially was a proposal that their police and the Krajina police would escort the group of 5.000 to the border of Croatia from where UNPROFOR should take over and escort the group to the border of Slovenia. Members of the group were then expected to proceed to Austria and Germany. The report goes on that we informed the Bosanski Novi representatives of various difficulties which the project raised in relation to the mandates of UNPROFOR and UNHCR. And with some difficulties we persuaded them of the need to speak with direct spokespersons of the group to ascertain their view. Two things: What was the difficulty that the project raised in relation to the mandates?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: This gentleman has a way of saying what I just said earlier in simple terms. The United Nations does not create refugees. We don't participate in the creation of refugees. We are trying to help them once they have been displaced but we wouldn't be in good stead with our mandate to participate in that process.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then secondly, the need to speak with direct spokespersons, was that again referring to the need to speak to representatives of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Exactly. If somebody is going to speak to me about 5.000, I need to know how connected they are to that 5.000 group.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Then I'll leave out the rest of this paragraph because it was effectively a discussion about the difficulties, and then 6, the situation, Mr. Rade, who did most of the talking for the visitors, explained that the majority of the population in Bosanski Novi is Serb, 60 per cent, and 33.5 per cent Muslim. The latter totalling some 13.000 pounds -- 13.000. Out of this group some 5.000 felt insecure and had addressed the authorities, mayor and police, for assistance to leave. And there was reportedly a convoy of 5.000 which would like to go to Austria and Germany where they had relatives. In order to help they had agreed for the Bosanski Novi police to escort them to the Croatia boundary. Then the Novi authorities had suggested to them to go to other parts of BH with a Muslim majority but they had refused, being afraid to be mobilised, and for the same reason, they did not wish to enter Croatia alone. Pausing there for a moment, did you make a note in your diary of this meeting, of the words that Mr. Pasic actually used when dealing with -- they didn't want to join the BiH Army and that they also didn't want to join the Croatian army? If you'd like to have a look at your entry, please, for that date, the 27th?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and as you read that text from this gentleman, it tracks pretty much my own notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then what did Mr. Pasic say about the Muslims declining to go to the other Muslim areas?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: The language I recorded in that regard says, "We suggested they go to central Bosnia where Muslims are majority." I'm reading my notes now, if they sound like the other text, it's as it should be. And I'm reading from my notes. "We suggested they go to central Bosnia where Muslims are majority, but they refused. They just want to go out of the fighting zones. They do not want to fight at all. They also have fear of Croatian authorities. They might be mobilised into the Croatian army. Our solution was for them to go to central Bosnia, since they refused that solution, we feel sorry and want to fulfil their wish." That is where -- as I wrote the notes it didn't sound genuine to me. At that moment, that was not a genuine statement. I wanted to probe it further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, exactly. You say you didn't -- it didn't sound genuine. So what did you go on to say?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Because remember, again, I want to put in context, this is how it flowed. I'm the person that they wanted to see in the meeting. I'm on a listening mode and also a talking mode while writing my notes. So that certain sequence of my text here would leave out what I said because I can't write and say at the same time and what the response was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: So at that stage, when I heard what I just wrote down, what I just read out, that there were -- we feel sorry and want to fulfil their wish, underscoring we want to fulfil their wish, I wanted to probe that where they what did you do and what caused them to want to go, and the answer was, in part, they were still in their houses, meaning the Muslims, and the other was a small -- they had a small convoy gathered in one place. At further probing, that it can't be that people want to leave their homes where they are security spontaneously, that's when I got an answer from the mayor Pasic that I quoted and it reads, "I admit that the Muslims have been under pressure of armed Serb irregulars."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did you understand by that reply?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: It considered to me what I thought all along, this is not a voluntary wish for the Muslims, and the Serbs are not fulfilling the wish of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And by the use of the term "Serbian irregulars" what did you understand by that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: At this moment, I just let it pass only understanding it's his way of saying don't look at me as the one who is causing this. It's somebody else. That's all I took it at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he explain to you at this stage that this pressure included shelling villages?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, as I said, I started probing this matter in greater details and my notes show a sequence. He went out to tell me a story beginning with how they formed their Serbian Republic, how they requested allegiance to come from Muslims, how they give them a date from which they were to either sign an allegiance and demobilise Muslims from these villages. When they refused to demobilise and brought dummy guns and all that, a long, long story.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's take it from your notes, I think, please?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've mentioned the Serbian irregulars?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And after that, did he give you the names of two Muslim spokespersons apparently?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: At this moment, remember he had come again to try to help me clear my incredulity, he still didn't have a Muslims around but later on he did bring two Muslims not at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, let's take it from your note. You told us he gave you a long account?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what he said?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, the elements of that account boiled down as follows: The authority of Bosanska Krajina - that's a reference, a Serbian reference to that area, of that - have decided that all armed troops should be disarmed. We proceeded to carry out this decision this way, meaning he was ordered by someone else under the authority quote Bosanska Krajina, and they all people who were not Serbs part of that government and were armed were to be disarmed, and they went on as follows. We held meetings of the SDS, Serbian party, and the SDA, the Muslims. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, pause there for a moment. Did he give a date for that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: The date of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The date of the meetings of the SDS and the --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: No, that one I don't have it on my notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Next?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: But second one, we held a meeting between 6 to 8th of May, I'm not sure it's the same as in point one but I see it as a bullet point 2 in my notes, and agreed all paramilitary groups should be disarmed in the municipality and set a deadline that the disarmament would be May 11th. Then we discussed a schedule of disarmament village by village. All settled for 9 to 10th of May. By then we would be expecting a disarmament. Third, SDS openly said at a meeting that they still -- no, SDA, SDA, openly said at the meeting that they still had arms. No arms were collected. The SDA being the Muslim side of these discussions. So all 5.000 come from the villages that did not disarm. So we are now -- I get clear, better and better, that all these 5.000 were Muslims who did not want to comply with these things that he is describing to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what he was telling you, that they refused to disarm?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes. The deadline was 11th of May. There were some provocations from the Muslims. We had information that they did not take seriously our request for disarmament. They brought a bag full of empty shells and five wooden rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So he's told you that apparently --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Late that night, they detected a military police patrol in the Blagaj village. This is the village where the group is gathered.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you say "they" who did you understand him -- this is what he was telling you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: This is all still Mayor Pasic talking.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So by they had detected a patrol who they, the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: They the Serbs, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then they detected this patrol in the village of Blagaj?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did he say anything else?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: That's where the 5.000 were gathered. And he said this region is under the authority of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina since May the 10th when the police control -- patrol was attacked, the conflict in the region began. Legal authorities forced the response against the Muslims and because of this, therefore now we are in this situation where these 5.000 people need to get out of here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did he give you a further description of what had happened to the Muslims or how the Serbs had dealt with them?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yeah. He went on to tell me some of the people have left their houses and have taken a few belongings, security was being provided by the army and police of the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he talk about Serbs giving any help to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Some, yes, he said some were being helped by the Muslims and being protected in some homes, yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he tell you that anyone had been hurt?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: No, I think he went out of his way to tell me at this moment that no one has -- nobody was being harmed at that moment, nobody was being hurt at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In this explanation did he tell you that by the response he was talking about the shelling of villages containing men, women and children which had forced these people to flee?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: At this moment, I wanted to understand my purpose of questioning him had delivered what I wanted so at this moment, I had been satisfied and he had admitted this is not a voluntary movement and that's really what I wanted to be clear. He understood that I understood and he did concede that was the purpose of my questioning him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If, however, he had indicated that this had been by means of shelling the villages with artillery, would you have made a note of that, do you think?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, if I had questioned him further than that, I would have noted that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. If we go back for a moment then to the report written by your colleague, we see at the top of the second page that within the last 15 to 20 days, the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina had also reached Bosanski Novi and there had been a certain amount of pressure from uncontrolled Serbian groups.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: What page is this, paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's paragraph second paragraph on the second page?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: He numbered his paragraphs, if you can go straight --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's part of paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's part of paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, yes, he's misnumbered it but it should be 4, clearly, Your Honour, it's the end of paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then clarifying questions effectively this covers the same ground as you covered in your note. Some are still in their houses, while others from three villages had formed a convoy in the village of Blagaj and according to the average Muslim village in the area, Muslim village in area, 5.000 would correspond to the depopulation of some ten villages. Members of the convoy, women, children, and men, had only taken with them what they could carry. Some houses said to have been damaged. Most supposed to belong to the Muslim party, and then again this question of protection taking into Serbian houses. Security at Blagaj said to be provided by the civil police and military police of the army of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina. These entities were formed by Serbians only since the Muslims had refused to sign a loyalty oath and accordingly voluntarily withdrew from service. And then in paragraph 6, we see again your colleague noting what you've just described to us, and then at the bottom of the page, we explained to the interlocutors that we had difficulties in understanding why a group of pacifists would not give up their arms and were informed that all 5.000 came from villages that did not disarm. So the point that -- that both of you were making was that you didn't understand if these were people who didn't want to fight in armies, why they didn't disarmed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: You see, I'm the one that was questioning them and my colleague basically was reporting what he heard from me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see, right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: And what I wanted to know from the mayor was, if they don't want to fight, and then they don't want to disarm, you can see those are two contradictory points. You tell me on the one hand they don't want to fight and then you tell me on the other hand they don't want to disarm, clearly something has to give. Why do you think it's so? And I have written note of his answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you had -- I was going to ask you. Could you tell us what he said?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: And he said and I quote, "The Muslims are not true pacifists, it's more a question of military weakness. They are afraid of revenge where they are a minority. Serbs minority in those areas were exposed to all kinds of atrocities by Muslims. Due to Izetbegovic's politics, they do not want to go in central Bosnia where they may be mobilised." So in other words, I understood that to mean that because they are weak in militarily, they really are not pacifists, they really can't stay here because we know if they were stronger they would fight. That's all he's saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you get the feeling as a result of what Mr. Pasic was saying that this movement of 5.000 was likely to be the last?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: No. And in fact that was my chief concerned. That's why I wanted the representatives of the UNHCR and ICRC to be there because this was just the beginning of something bigger and a point you made earlier, we are talking about 5.000 people gathered in Blagaj. By the Mayor Pasic himself informs me there were 13.000 people making up the population of that village, 13.000, and the majority were Muslim so if he is saying 5.000 have to go with this explanation, you don't need to be a rocket scientist to know that the rest of them will have to go too and that bothered me if you start it you're going to get a flood of people coming from there. We already been given the percentages of Muslims making up a village like Bosanska Krupa, the majority one, so I'm being served notice this is round one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You said 13.000 in the village. You meant in the municipality, I think?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: No, no, no, village of Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think if you look at back at -- if you look at paragraph 6 -- what is numbered paragraph 6 but should be 4, the 13.000 I think referred to the population this Muslim population of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: That is my colleague talking. I'm looking at my own notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: And I'm saying that the Muslim population of 13.000 in total have asked local authorities for protection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So as far as you can see, this is opening the -- or attempting to open the floodgates and you said you required your colleagues from the other relief organisations to be there. What was your final response to Mr. Pasic about what you were prepared to do?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: It was clear and my colleagues on UNHCR whose docket of responsibilities would reflect is with all due respect to you as mayor we are not going to really go along with this. This is not something we are willing to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Pasic -- what was his reaction when you told him you weren't going to go along with this?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: It was funny because at that moment he decided that to ask me who my boss is, if I'm not going to accept it, he said Mr. Kirudja who is your boss so that -- it's obvious that you don't understand what the issues are so can you tell us who your boss is so we can go and talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now at the bottom of the note of the meeting made my your colleague, there is a reference to -- this is at paragraph 9 -- obviously quoting you throughout the meeting we insisted on learning of the situation directly from the representatives of the group. And after much hesitation, two were named. And then we see the names of the gentlemen. It says president of the Muslim national organisation -- should that be SDA? I think it looks like SDR?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: No that should be SDA my colleague made an error there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. The claimed originator of the wish to move. And then another one. We also asked for representatives of local NGOs, we would be able to talk with those persons if they could come to Dvor. And then in discussing the right of the representatives to speak with us directly, and participate in informing them of the situation and in decisions relating to them, CAC, and that's you, I think, is it not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was blunt in saying we should stop pretending that the persons were leaving voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was admitted by the representatives if we met with these persons directly we would hear that they did not want to leave.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: That's precisely -- and that was the intention of my meeting to lay to rest that repeated thing that they are moving voluntarily. I wanted that to be laid to rest at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so was that at that stage how the matter was left?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: It was. And I also note that those two representatives you read item 2 were already in the meeting of -- of the date that is shown here, and in subsequent meetings later, you may see references to others with different names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, thank you. We can leave that document now which I think is already exhibited. And can we move next to a document dated the 6th of June? It's Exhibit P1662. Actually, I'm sorry, in time, I'm sorry, can I have document please, P1661 first? I'm so sorry because that's first in time. And then 662.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this report, I think was signed not by -- or was forwarded not by you but also -- but by your subordinate, Mr. Raffone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's got writing on the top, is that your writing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: No, none of this is my writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: None of this is your writing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you -- it's quite difficult to read. I don't know whether -- you may be more familiar with your colleague's writing, it would be important for what is it UNHCR to resume its activities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Activities, yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the next word?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Interruption was due --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To the fact that they could only reach...

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Me -- is it our side?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No that can't be right, one side, the Serbs, yes, thank you, however, it seems now feasible to reach something or other areas, Muslim areas, such as Bihac. All right can we just look then at the report that Mr. Raffone forwarded, 6th of June, 1992, but -- is the date of this one but it says phone call from the mayor -- I'm sorry, I'll start that again, "Subject, potential Muslim refugees from BH. A, phone call from the mayor of Banja Luka. On the 1st of June, 1992, the mayor of Banja Luka, Mr. Kupresanin, called the civil affairs office in Sector North. He conveyed some information concerning the Muslims refugee -- the Muslim refugees flow that might originate from his area towards Croatia passing through the crossing points in Dvor and Karlovac. The mayor's information can be summarised as follows: The mayors of Bosanski Novi, Prijedor, Kljuc, Dubica, Sanski Most and the one in Banja Luka had contacts about the situation of the Muslim population in the area." Now the next sentence has gone completely haywire but it's something like the Muslim population something or other it looks like?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Fears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fears persecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ah, that's no better?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: From the Serb militia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "From the Serb militia in the area. No more food or medical supplies are available for the Muslim population. The Muslim population do not trust the Serb local authorities which have enforced a one-sided disarmament in the area. The Muslims have tried to enter the Croatian-controlled town of Travnik but were not allowed to. And then the mayor estimates that some 15.000 persons have already left their normal place of residence, moving towards Dvor and some more 15.000 might follow in a short time. The mayor launched an appeal to UNPROFOR and the western countries to find a way to protect the Muslim civil population and deliver urgently -- urgent humanitarian aid in the area." Now, was this a phone call that you had taken or that Mr. Raffone had taken?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: This was a phone call taken by Mr. Raffone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And just -- presume -- did you speak Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Myself?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, or Mr. Raffone speak either of you speak Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Not that -- you learned a phrase here and there by the fly but we were totally at the mercy of our interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was going to ask?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who provided your interpreters?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: We had several local people employed in our office, enough to do that for every officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And so the fact that this gentleman is described as the mayor of Banja Luka would have been what the interpreter interpreted to Mr. Raffone?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yeah, they were not meeting face to face and as far as I know we had never been to Banja Luka. I never sent Mr. Raffone there so he wouldn't be speaking of personal knowledge of the man up to that time when he received the call.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then we see humanitarian concern, and it deals with effectively what was -- is described as humanitarian emergency need in Bihac?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then if we go over the page please to political issues, "The problem of the Muslim enclave in the Bihac area is a key element for understanding of the political issues presented by the Serb authorities in Knin and its links with the so-called Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As a matter of fact, the Muslim enclave has been encircled by a large territory controlled by Serbs, north and west by Sector North, south and east by SRBH. And the Serb authorities in the areas around the Muslim enclave are sending messages to UNPROFOR to highlight the danger that might occur if a massive exodus of Muslims begins." And then there are certain -- deals with -- perhaps I should read the whole thing. "In fact these messages have been conveyed to civil affairs officers by local authorities in Sector North as well as by the local authorities in BH. All messages are warning that the exodus of Muslims towards Sector North could provoke tensions amongst the Serb population and that UNPROFOR should provide assistance to them in order to guarantee their security in the UNPA. The displaced Muslim community appears to have become a pawn in the hands of the Serb communities in the UNPAs and BH. Other armed Muslim elements and Croatian armed units -- I'm sorry, pawn in the hands of them. And some earlier signals of this have been observed during conversations with local authorities in the UNPA and in Croatia." When you referred to the Bihac enclave, were you referring not just to Bihac itself but the other parts that you pointed out?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Indeed. And if you permit me, this report, you can see was released by my -- under my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: The timing is also June. We have been there already the shape of the things to come and present at that time was complete. We referred to that area at times as Bihac pocket, a pocket is indicative of enclose. We used the word as an enclave to again signal the total area being surrounded, that area with a population of 250.000 to 300.000 people in that area. It is useful to bear in mind, later on that understanding became complete, even at the headquarters of the UN when Bihac became one of those enclaves of protected areas, it was named along Srebrenica and others as an UN protected zone so this was building towards that understanding, and the shape of that understanding had already materialised at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You can leave that and then please now go to Exhibit P1662.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, Ms. Korner, let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, I take note of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is a report also dated the 6th of June and if we go, please, to the subject matter of the memorandum that was enclosed, have you got that? It's been copied on the other side, right. The subject being displaced persons from Bosanski Novi referred to in yesterday's military sit-rep. The duty officer at DanCon and I think later on we'll see that sit-rep in a collection of documents, in Kostajnica, informed the -- informed you, Mr. Kirudja, I think, over the telephone that the 1900 hours sit-rep will report as follows, about the 350 displaced persons reported to have been gathered in a football field in Bosanski Novi. The 350 persons were seen to be loaded on to buses to unknown destination in Bosnia. They are no longer at the football stadium. DanCon had no knowledge of who was loading the person into buses. At no time did they cross the River Una into the UNPA, i.e. into Dvor or the surrounding area. Is that why the conclusion was drawn that they had gone somewhere in Bosnia with these 350 people?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, but also it is again like the purpose of all these memos is to inform and clarify things going on at my own headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: This memo was responding to something coming from headquarters tell us where they are going, what are they doing, something like that, and I'm giving -- I'm trying to clarify things my own headquarters wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Then comment, the Bosnian border with the UNPA has very rapidly become a flash point for both displaced persons and what local authorities on this side call terrorist infiltrators, in inverted commas, the trouble sports run from Bihac, Cazin, Bosanska Krupa, Bosanski Novi, Velika Kladusa, Prijedor, and Banja Luka, all within Bosnia. When the --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: That's my boss, my boss's deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Telephoned about this subject, the civil affairs office was in the process of preparing a message to UNHCR in Zagreb on a letter from the President of the Bihac district assembly, assessed to the SC?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Sector command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On a matter that could result in similar displacement of mostly Muslim population. Further, a second message in progress is about a telephone call from the mayor of Banja Luka conveying a similar message about Muslim refugees originating from along the flash points named. And I trust the forthcoming messages will help to clarify what is going on along the border. We have looked at that message. Now, where were you getting the information that -- the trouble spots that you named there, in particular, Prijedor and Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Again, if you look at the chronology, there were previous reports beginning with the very first one you put into evident this morning of a woman coming from Bosanski Novi. I just -- stream and bits of information that is being reported of people escaping in various numbers at varying times. Each time, as you notice that each time we met these people, in the process of giving them humanitarian assistance, we would debrief them. What is it is causing to you leave your homes? Where are you going? Who is behind what you report to be a problem? So -- and the town's name, the places, the circumstances, were building up and these towns that we have named kept on cropping from different individuals and the different circumstances. And that's how it is summarised as these are the flash points.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally on this document, was this the first time you'd heard of this football field in Bosanski Novi, apparently containing some kind of detainees there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: No, as reported in the document in front of me, it is not the first time. This is the first time the headquarters, my own headquarters is focusing on this story.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right, okay. I'm sorry, yes, you'd obviously been informed that day but had there been any mention of people being kept in a football field before around this period, the 6th of June?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: I'm not sure that -- if I have the date of the flash point report itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We will see that at a later --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: That is the date when the matter came to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Fine, thank you, Mr. Kirudja, that's all I ask you about that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm going to move on to the next report so perhaps that would be a convenient moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect. We will have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner? We wait -- where is the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I've had a pleading message, it was more of an order from the interpreters please to leave a pause between the question and answer over the break so I'm going to try and if you can try as well to pause after I've asked the question before you answer?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not you. It's me, I can assure you. Could you be handed now, please the document this was marked P1666? This, Mr. Kirudja, was a report that you forwarded on the 9th of June, again in respect of this issue of those 5.000 Muslims, and the second page, I think, is a note, and it's a report that you received from UNHCR. And again we needn't trouble with the names of the people involved. Dated -- it looks like the 5th of June and it says that the Zagreb office was today visited by two gentlemen, I don't think again we need their names, who came to provide further information on the situation of the 5.000 Muslims in Bosanski Novi, and the present note supplements my report of the 29th of May, 1992. Both visitors are originally from Bosanski Novi. It describes the circumstances of these visitors -- I might as well -- Mr. Cehajic was a retired migrant worker in Slovenia but he had gone back to Bosanski Novi and managed to escape when the convoy was formed. And then it described the escape route. "He confirmed that the disarmament of the Muslim villages had taken place. He was in the village of Suhaca and had been the first one to lay down arms. When they had done that, some Serbian territorial military moved in, together with Krajina police, and told them to leave the houses. The houses were searched while the villagers waited in the field for five to six hours. After the search, they were allowed back and told they would be all right. However, a few days after, the first shelling started, a grenade landed in his yard. Shelling was by cannons and mortars from neighbouring Serb villages. The informant did not know of any agreement on disarmament, had not been involved, nor had he knowledge of any symbolic denouncement of an agreement." The writer of this report clearly was dealing with a the matters that had been said to you at that meeting. "He noted that no Serb had been killed in this area. Serbian villages had not been disarmed. Rather helicopters had come in with supplies from Banja Luka and Knin." Paragraph 5. "On the 23rd of May, 1992, the villages of Donji Agici, Gornji Agici, and Hozici was burned, presumably were burned, on Sunday, the 24th of May, a big convoy was formed from six villages. Peoples felt compelled to flee because their villages were destroyed. In his village, Suhaca, the fires had been started on the edges of the village to frighten people out. He had also seen Hozici on fire. He had heard reports on the destruction of other villages and believed the process to be going on. The convoy had formed in two groups and he did not know how far the first one had gone. The main convoy was stopped in Blagaj by persons in Serbian military uniforms, just like JNA, and Serb paramilitary groups. From symbols on their uniform, it was deduced that they should be under control of the Serbian Democratic Party and Mayor Pajic. That presumably should be Pasic. The Serbs at Blagaj had wanted to mobilise both men and women, supposedly the convoy had also been promised free passage in order to clean the area." And then he managed to escape on the 24th of May. "Conditions in Blagaj believed to be bad and with no food, the informant had managed to make some telephone contacts. The Cazin crisis board did not know anything of the convoy. No press and media is allowed into the territory. On the 1st of June, he heard from Bosanska Dubica that Suhaca and Hozici were on fire and that there had been massacres in those two villages, 52 deaths. "I mentioned the two names given to us as spokespersons for the group, those are the one that is were in that report, they were believed to be imprisoned or kept with the men as hostages in the school in Blagaj. This information had come over the telephone from Sisak from some men who had escaped. Mr. Izet Muhamed -- I had trouble with this earlier, Muhamedagic was named as the contact person in the letter from the 1st of June but it is not known where he is. Action desired: The two visitors differed somewhat in what they hoped to be done. It was common ground that they would like someone to go to the area and to see what was going on. There was no armed conflict in the area which on surface is calm. They would like to see an intervention to free the Muslims and get them to a safe area in their homes or somewhere else. And that the other gentleman was explicit in preferring the last option at least for women and children. He believed family members in Croatia and Slovenia could help take care of them." When you got this, Mr. Kirudja, did you consider this was an important amount of information you were being given?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes. And as you can see, he had addressed it first party as is headquarters reporting office and to me because of where he was operating from.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: An office of UNPROFOR. The importance I attached to and therefore while he could send his own report directly to his headquarters, I needed to at the same time send his report to my own headquarters, in the process, as is evident from the paragraphs you have read, it would collaborate already a pattern of information from other sources already conveyed to my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in fact, I think I have by an error missed a report that I'd like you to look at, please. In fact we have to go back in time. Could you look, please, at a document that was number 13 of the documents? I'm sorry, yes, it's going to -- don't worry, I've forgotten, it's included in a later bundle but I think you're going to need it at this stage to follow the story chronologically. Could you have a look, please, at P1669? Now, that contains as we'll see later on, but that contains a number of documents that you -- because you bundled together everything that had been dealt with on this topic. Usher if you could give it to me, I'll find the one that I want the witness to look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the document -- if you -- it's got fax numbers at the top, if you notice, and it's P -- it's the 15th page on the fax. It's an UNPROFOR, United Nations protections force in Yugoslavia, and this goes back to what Mr. Kirudja was saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a document addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dated the 6th of June from Mr. Thornberry?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it says, "Please investigate immediately and in coordination with CIVPOL and advise urgently on the following: The 6th of June sit-rep indicates that one of Dan patrols, Danish patrols, I suppose, observed 100 women and children being brought into stadium with their heads covered with clothes and carrying plastic bags with ten armed persons guarding stadium. CIVPOL here will be giving instructions to their personnel." Did you yourself write something on that document?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes. On the left side of that document, it was a note which had the effect of causing the civil police units in the sector to begin to investigate on the subject what they knew, what they could find out. That was the intent and purpose of that note to the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just read what it says? CIVPOL chief of op?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, undertake to instruct the completion -- the station chief, Kostajnica, this morning at Vojnic to investigate -- to investigate the report -- the report, all have to complete tomorrow a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will have complete.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in other words I wanted them to undertake the reported requested by Mr. Thornberry and give me their findings by the next morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, if you go, please, then, to the next document, which I think you'll find on the back of it, which is a report dated the 8th of June, signed by yourself?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Investigative report on the displaced people observed in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Reference your subject message dated the 6th of June, as indicated in an earlier message, the people observed as being held in the stadium at Bosanski Novi have been relocated elsewhere in Bosnia. A CIVPOL report from Dvor will be dispatched. Then you describe where Bosanski Novi is, and the story appearing in the DanCon sit-rep was observed from Dvor, what they think they saw seems to be the tip of a political iceberg. And then you talk about the meeting with yourself and the mayor of Dvor but you draw your own conclusions from it because you said, "It became clear from the meeting that the mayor of Bosanski Novi, Mr. Pasic, and the mayor of Dvor, Mr. Borojevic were acting in a common cause to the following effect: A, cause a massive evacuation under the guise of humanitarian assistance of some 5.000 residents of Bosanski Novi as discussed in greater detail below. And talk UNPROFOR into accepting responsibility for the transit of the 5.000 people through the UNPA and out to Slovenia. In the process, the two mayors would contact their receptive governments, in inverted commas who would arrange for the presence of international TV coverage of the voluntary, inverted commas, and humanitarian, inverted commas, evacuation of pacifists inverted commas Muslims, destination Germany and Austria." Then you describe the meeting on the 27th of May you concluded that the mayor had collaborated in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and was acting on their behalf and as you already told us admitted -- he admitted that the Muslims were not really leaving voluntarily but were under duress from Serbian armed irregulars. And again, then you set out what you already told us. Just want to check my note on something else. Yes. Now, thank you. Can you be handed, please, Exhibit P1664?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Could you, counsel, allow me a comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Mr. Kirudja, I thought we had dealt with it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: No. If it would help the Court. I would like the Court to note -- I knew you spoke about the importance of my notes. This document will illustrate a point I made and applies generally. My notes were always intended to be reproduced in content into the official document that I wrote. As you can see yourself and the testimony when I was reading the notes, that pretty much the complete of what was in the notes in this official report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: So you shouldn't conclude there is anything else left in my notes of importance that you haven't got in either the official notes or in testimony, and that applies in general, as far as my notes are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman is delighted to hear that, I'm sure. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now can we look, please, at the document all around this was clearly a time of great activity, dated the 8th of June again, and you sent a further message to your headquarters. A memorandum dated the 8th of June, subject, appeal for humanitarian help to 250.000 Muslims from the President of the Bihac district assembly. And you describe the letter which you also attach, and in the second paragraph, you describe you attached the letter, "As you may have seen from two messages to our headquarters in Belgrade copied to you, the situation on the border between the UNPA and BH has rapidly become a flash point for displaced persons as well as attacks and counterattacks by armed units. We are aware of UNHCR's decision to suspend operations in BH." And then you describe the conversation you had with ICRC as well, who also suspended their operations. "In the absence of both UNHCR and ICRC from the areas in question, UNPROFOR is the only address for the local people in distress. And as you know, UNPROFOR has neither the money, the means, nor the mandate to respond to such humanitarian crisis in the making." And there is an appeal to the other organisations to reconsider. Bihac is a largely Muslim enclave. It is encircled in all directions by Serbian controlled territories. The area around Bihac could be self-supporting if some ways of communication could be opened to allow the transit of supplies and external trade. And then you talk about the humanitarian help required and finally end up by saying this: "Recent events in the area of Bosanski Novi should sound an alarm to international humanitarian agencies." By this stage, at the beginning of June, what was the influx of refugees like?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: You would call it, if I may use a weather metaphor, it started with a drizzle and was becoming a torrent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was that from all areas of BH?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: You would particularly be more accurate to say there was already flash points in the areas named, the towns mentioned constantly, Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Krupa, Prijedor, Kljuc, Sanski Most, and the rest of those areas, they seemed to have been the focal points of where whatever was causing these refugees to come seems to be focused on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I want to ask you about that report. I want to move now please to a meeting that you had on the 13th of June with a Mr. Junic, the deputy mayor of Dvor and other people. Now, on this occasion, I think you'll need to consult your diary about this because I think the issue of the football field was raised.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: June 13?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: June the 13th.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there was a meeting, I think there were a number of issues discussed but could you find the part of your note where the football field was raised by the deputy mayor?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours this is page 22 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was a meeting covering a lengthy discussions in various matters, at the end of which the mayor focused on the issue of the people gathered or being made to gather at that football field.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you recorded was discussed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Just as well I read it aloud what my note says. The fact was that there were people brought into the football field. Their houses were searched while they were in the field. When their houses had been searched, those whose houses did not have weapons were allowed to go back. Some resisted during the transport to the football field. They were arrested. They were the same who had weapons in their houses. Those in houses were those who voluntarily wanted to fight for the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they were taken by buses to Banja Luka. When they arrived, the local authorities did not let them in and returned them to Bosanski Novi. The Banja Luka authorities said they will request them to come back when they needed them. At the moment, they are free and in their own houses. This problem will persist, says the mayor, until the next round when a draft into the army of Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that the end of your note?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: That's the first part of the paragraph I was listening to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: I myself said something, then he responds.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you said?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: See, at that moment, you realise again I was always required, being an official of United Nations, to establish a basis of why something is being brought up to me. Once again, this is the deputy mayor of Dvor. He is talking to me in great detail about things in Bosanski Novi, outside the jurisdiction of where he is mayor, so I must have reminded him again of the oddity of him talking to me about this. Of course by then I began to concede that the Serbs in Bosanski Dvor made no difference as to whether their government, their so-called government, was in part of Croatia or extended across the boundary. So I asked him a number of questions and he said okay, we will pass them all back to the mayor of Bosanski Novi and he will respond to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That was the question I was going to ask. Did he explain why he was raising the deputy mayor of Dvor, I think it was a Mr. Junic, was raising the problem of the football field people?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: As I said to you earlier, counsel, when you asked me, it's at the end of a number of issues raised all around, touching on all kinds of directions, and it triggered the issue of the football field.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So he told you that he was going to pass the questions you had?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- back to Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now can we look, please, at the next report in time that you wrote, dated the 16th of June, Exhibit 1668? Entitled humanitarian disaster in the making in Bihac and along the Bosnia border. The first paragraph stated that "The humanitarian situation in Bihac is rapidly deteriorating. There was a meeting on the 1st of June at the request of the UNMOs and the mayor of Bihac. Armed elements in the area terrorised the population on both sides of the border, a stream of vindictive killings, forced mass movement of persons and other horrible reprisals have been reported to UNPROFOR. And the only independent source of information on the area is the UNMOs base in Bihac." I read this out on a number of occasions. Can you just explain to the court just in case we have not mentioned this what an UNMO was?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: A very -- a very uniquely United Nations concept of dealing with issues of mandate as well as the reality of areas where we are operating. As you noticed, the major forces, that means fighting forces of the UN battalions, contingents, were fully deployed inside the United Nations Protected Areas, meaning where the Security Council had issued a mandate for the deployment of those forces. But the reality was such that even if you formed a border or confrontation line, there were effectively spilling over areas where you are said not to have a mandate, meaning outside those boundaries. The UN was organised therefore with the concurrence of all the parties in the conflict to allow United Nations Military Observers to be based and located outside areas otherwise you would claim we have no mandate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: That's the importance and meaning of saying UNMO's. In that case they were located in Bihac which is outside the UNPA and in Velika Kladusa, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, as we already saw, you said that the ICRC and UNHCR had temporarily suspended their operations. Three, an immediate humanitarian relief operation in Bihac has become a necessity to aid the residents, most of whom are Muslims, out of the desperate conditions. Such an operation would have to be organised taking into account that the Bihac area is presently nearly impossible to supply with overland convoys from Sarajevo or Zagreb unless the latter are escorted by heavy armed units. And then you go on to describe the alternative methods of supply, I suppose, plus some killings that had taken place in Dvor and an area near Velika Kladusa. And then -- yes, you say, in Cazin, the local TDF authorities, that's the Territorial Defence forces, I take it -- claim Muslims axed 40 Serbians to death in the last two days. None of these stories have been verified by independent sources. They seem however to be part of a concerted action by Serbian leaders on both sides of the border to isolate the Muslims in the area. And then you go on to describe the difficulties of relief, describe the town of Bihac, the fact that the Serbs had left it and controlled the main road, and that Bihac had been shelled and Muslim villages evacuated or liberated by Serbian forces. And therefore, and I imagine this was your concern particularly, the number of displaced persons and refugees is dramatically increasing. Paragraph 6, the Serbs appear to be intent on demilitarising the Muslims in the area. Rumours of forced displacements and summary executions are slowly reaching outsiders. Political talks were going on until the 6th of June, 1992 between the leaders of the SDS and the SDA and since then, the Serbs have reportedly suspended participation in the talks with the Muslims. The SDS president, Mr. Bjelac reportedly prepared a document in consultation with the Serbian authorities in Banja Luka to be forwarded to the Muslim authorities in Bihac. And the UNMOs interpret this text as an ultimatum to the town of Bihac. Basically the document dictates conditions to the Muslims giving the option of a soft border or a hard border. Before we go on to the next part, we are going to see other references to Serbian authorities in Banja Luka. You never went to Banja Luka but how much did what was the authorities in Banja Luka appear to impact on the people you were dealing with?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Remember, mine was a much broader interaction from the military side to the humanitarian side, we had to look at this whole issue, moving as fast as it was moving. One of the things I kept track of, meticulously, is this changes in the military command of the Serbs and where they moved and where they were in the sector and outside, there was rapidly moving scenario. In Knin, also in particular, and by this time I believe, and I'm not sure the details are clear to my mind, I believe certain command, certain exchange of command, of military, between Banja Luka and Knin, I believe may have been the general who used to command -- have command in first Krajina, based in Banja Luka, be moved in Knin and so forth. So the role of Banja Luka was something we took care of watching. Secondly, you talked to me about the corridor. That corridor, one of the point of that corridor is Banja Luka, a central point, where not only you have to pass through but most people stop there for a day or two, coming from the sector into Belgrade. So that was part of the reason we paid attention to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then the report goes on about an ultimatum received by -- from Muslim leaders. Is that right? 14th of June, the TDF commander informed the sector commander and yourself that an ultimatum was received from the Muslim leaders telling all Muslims living in Kordun to pick up their stuff and return to Bosnia. I take it that should be "to"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Again, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 8?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The TDF commander informed the sector commander and the CAC, that's yourself, that an ultimatum was received "from" Muslim leaders in the villages, and you name them, both in Cazin, telling all Muslims living in Kordun to pick up their stuff and return to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: Yes. It's correct the way it's stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From was it? So Muslims were saying to other Muslims go back to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: That's what the Serbs were saying to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see, all right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
utterances.text: The Serbs were saying to me we have received a Muslim ultimatum and that was a summary of a bigger story as always in these reports are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA.
